Replay

Replay checkpoint replication

9 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
Ownership and integrationShared gameplay connectionTransfer and retention protocolEvidence and limitsIndependent application consumersSchema-aware checkpoint compressionCheckpoint delivery channel

replay/recovery transfers complete authority checkpoints to an explicitly trusted successor. It builds on replay/net archives and the borrowed transport interface. Use it to keep an eligible backup ready before a host stops. It provides transfer, validation and retention. It does not select a legitimate leader, prevent an isolated old authority from committing, discover a new host, or reconnect game clients.

The reusable transfer package also supports bounded canonical records, exposed through recovery's Sender / Blob_Receiver facade types. Supply the expected envelope kind and an accept(user, archive, bytes) -> bool callback to blob_init; opt the Sender into the same kind with archive_kind. The core verifies source/scope, chunks, SHA-256 and envelope integrity before the callback. The callback must validate and install atomically, borrow bytes only for its duration, and return false on failure. Receipts are retained for retry handling; the generic core does not retain decoded application values. The typed checkpoint Receiver wraps this core and still retains the two validated authority checkpoints required by the sender/coordinator contract. Both receiver owners must stay at stable addresses. These types use the existing checkpoint APIs and canonical archive format. Optional transfer representations require negotiated peer support.

The P2P spectator uses the generic core for confirmed history; its separate envelope kind cannot be installed as an authority checkpoint.

Ownership and integration#

The application installs Scope{room, epoch, binding, content} and a specific transport peer on each endpoint. A binding identifies a particular authorized source/successor connection. Replace the binding when reconnecting/replacing that peer, even if the transport reuses its numeric ID. These identifiers are context checks, not credentials or authentication. A successor receives the complete authority projection, including hidden fields; select it accordingly.

Odin
sender: recovery.Sender
receiver: recovery.Receiver(World, Control, Action, Event, SEATS)
error := recovery.sender_init(&sender, scope, successor_peer, wire)
error = recovery.receiver_init(&receiver, scope, authority_peer, wire, model)

// Authority side: capture at a simulation boundary, then publish an owned copy.
error = recovery.sender_publish(&sender, &checkpoint, model, now_ms)

// Each endpoint's packet dispatcher, after transport.poll/receive:
result := recovery.receiver_receive(&receiver, packet.from, packet_bytes, now_ms)
// Or sender_receive on the publishing endpoint.
error = recovery.receiver_update(&receiver, now_ms)
// Or sender_update on the publishing endpoint.

Check every error/result. Call sender_destroy/receiver_destroy once; neither closes the borrowed transport. Owners must remain at stable addresses and must not be shallow-copied. sender_begin accepts encoded archive bytes and copies them; sender_publish encodes a typed checkpoint first. Only one transfer is active per sender. sender_cancel permits explicit replacement while retaining the last validated receipt; sequences continue increasing within the binding.

The low-level protocol does not independently drain the wire. Link integrates it with the gameplay runner using transport.Router, separate queues, and a combined output budget. handles inspects packet framing for routing without validating or trusting the payload. The standalone ENet acceptance fixture uses a dedicated wire; the cave replication gate uses the same connection for actual gameplay and checkpoints.

Shared gameplay connection#

Link(State, Control, Action, Event, Seats) owns the router, one outgoing transfer, an optional incoming receiver, and reusable archive schema metadata. Initialize it around the underlying transport, then give link_game_transport to server_init or client_init. Each outer frame calls link_pump once, pumps/steps gameplay, and finally calls link_server or link_client. Destroy the link before closing the underlying transport. The Godot Session facade performs this ordering.

Receiver opt-in is explicit: set Link_Config.accept_checkpoints=true. The authority then calls link_target with a live admitted connection. Use net.server_seat_connection when selecting by playable seat. The binding comes from the admission ledger's connection generation; it cannot be supplied by an incoming archive. The target interval defaults to one simulation second. New archives wait for the active transfer to complete/fail, avoiding endless replacement of partial transfers. Retargeting and link_untarget discard that target's current receipt; sequence numbers keep increasing so selecting the same live peer again does not collide with old transfers.

The link does not automatically reauthorize a replacement connection. A disconnected, kicked, or generation-mismatched target receives no further work. Its old receipt remains inspectable along with an unavailable status. Selecting a new live connection is an explicit application/coordinator decision. Incoming archives remain available after connection loss for the eventual takeover driver.

Packet routing preserves sender identity and delivery mode. Only bounded checkpoint messages enter the background queue; every consumer still validates its own protocol. Queue overflow may drop unreliable background datagrams, which the transfer repairs. Reliable background messages use the router's bounded retention/backpressure path. Combined byte/rate budgets reserve capacity for gameplay; a saturated game may defer checkpoints until their timeout. The most recent backup failure remains in Link.error/model_error; it does not halt active gameplay. The migration driver must consider checkpoint age and successor availability rather than assume a fresh replica always exists. Custom policy validators must be installed before receiver initialization, with an immutable user descriptor valid for the receiver's lifetime.

receiver_latest returns the newest validated receipt. receiver_checkpoint looks up an exact archive descriptor and returns a read-only borrow, valid until the next receive/destroy. The takeover driver must use the receipt authorized by the coordinator; newest does not by itself mean authorized. The archive can be passed to net.server_restore or persisted by an application.

By default, a saved custom admission policy is rejected. Install policy_valid and its immutable user descriptor to explicitly validate the policy ID/data before acknowledgement. The application must also provide the corresponding admission implementation during restore. Policy bytes never deserialize callbacks.

Transfer and retention protocol#

Protocol v1 uses canonical RPLY envelopes with kinds 0x5101–0x5105:

Message Meaning
Offer Version/chunk size, room/binding, archive sequence/tick/size/SHA-256, and last acknowledged archive to retain
Chunk Archive sequence and chunk index followed by exactly the expected bytes
Progress Offer receipt, or a 64-chunk acknowledgement bitmap
Ready Exact descriptor of a fully reconstructed and validated archive
Failed Explicit integrity/archive/policy/retention/timeout failure

Transfers use 1,024-byte chunks. The largest packet is 1,102 bytes, within the configured test datagram limit. On the unreliable transport channel, a bounded selective-repeat window repairs lost chunks and progress messages. Repeated offers repair lost Ready packets. ACKs cannot claim chunks that were never sent. Packet checksums protect framing; the final SHA-256 identifies the complete archive. Neither provides peer authentication.

The receiver preallocates one 1 MiB reassembly buffer, with fixed bitmaps. Offers cannot allocate arbitrary buffers. Bounds, version, scope, exact chunk length, duplicate consistency, final digest, checkpoint codec, game-state validity, and custom policy support are checked before a Ready receipt. Timeouts apply at receive as well as update, so a late final chunk cannot bypass the deadline.

Two validated archives may be retained. Each new offer names the authority's last acknowledged archive as its retention anchor. A newer candidate whose Ready was lost may be superseded, while that older anchor remains available. Validation uses a temporary third checkpoint; only a successful decode changes stored owners. An incomplete, corrupt, rejected, or timed-out transfer cannot replace a usable archive. Unknown retention claims are rejected. A completed transfer is a receipt for validated process memory, not a disk/power-loss guarantee. The successor must remain available, or another eligible replica is required.

Stats records packets/bytes, retries, duplicate chunks, deferral, rejection, validation, and failures. Receipts include archive tick and receipt time; the game can calculate checkpoint age. The caller supplies monotonic milliseconds; time reversal is rejected. CPU measurements belong around the calls so the pure package does not depend on an operating-system clock or Godot.

Evidence and limits#

Shell
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_recovery/run.sh
nix develop --command bash tests/replay_recovery_enet/run.sh

Nine native tests cover receipt/restore/action identity, lost Ready and retention, invalid state, timeout and recovery, same-archive connection rebinding, wrong peers, corrupt packets, time reversal, custom policies, offer limits/version/retention, out-of-range chunks, and a large private cave archive under deterministic faults. The integration test runs gameplay plus repeated archives, checks that an unselected observer receives none, retargets the same connection, and revokes the target. The package and actual Godot probe also type-check for WASM. This is not a browser network runtime gate; ENet is still native-only.

The real two-process ENet fixture transfers a cave simulation with looted inventory and an active rock, plus 72,000 bytes of authority-only fixture data. With 120 ms receive delay, up to 20 ms jitter, 10% unreliable loss, and 10% duplication, one debug-build run recorded:

Text
archive: 75,591 bytes, tick 49
capture/encode: 39,591 us
transfer through Ready: 2,043 ms, 173,838 sent bytes, 95 retries
receiver packet processing/validation: 193,712 us accumulated
restore and first continued simulation tick: 108,260 us

The restored complete frame equals the transferred checkpoint, includes the private data and conserved loot, and continues simulation. These are single-run instrumentation receipts, not percentile benchmarks or old/new game comparisons. The fixture adds private data specifically to exceed the 64 KiB packet limit; ordinary Cavecrawl archives are smaller. Those measurements motivated reusable net.Checkpoint_Codec metadata. Receivers initialize and cache it at startup; Link prepares its publishing codec when a target is selected. The same fixture with cached metadata recorded 1,574 us capture/encode and 7,304 us accumulated receiver processing, with identical archive bytes. One-time fresh server restore still builds its runtime schemas (139,521 us in that run). These remain individual debug measurements.

The first Godot debug build terminated inside the Odin compiler. Direct debug, non-debug, and the subsequent normal project build succeeded without a source workaround; the crash has not been reproduced or claimed fixed.

The live Cavecrawl gate is examples/replay_cavecrawl/replication_run.sh. It keeps gameplay and periodic backups on the same ENet connection, with the same fault settings, and verifies a common checkpoint containing the guest's loot and open door. Save/resume and restarted-host/guest recovery gates remain separate.

The Room driver installs coordinator-approved successor and fencing decisions, then performs planned or abrupt takeover with surviving-client frontier reconciliation. See the recovery contract and roadmap for its guarantees and remaining work.

Independent application consumers#

link_add_application(&config, Application_Route{user, handles}) reserves another bounded receive lane before link_init. It returns (lane, ok); adding an identical route is idempotent and a full registry returns false. Obtain that borrowed lane with link_application_lane(&link, lane). The original application_handles and link_application_transport retain lane 2, so existing asset consumers continue to work. Extra routes use lanes 3–7, with the same router budgets and primary reserve.

Classification is ordered: checkpoint, original application, additional routes, then gameplay fallback. Handlers should match only their own protocol. Routing is not authentication; each consumer validates live admission and scope. All enabled consumers must drain their lanes after the shared pump. A full reliable receive lane preserves its packet and can exert transport backpressure. Comms uses an additional route while Session assets keep their existing one.

Schema-aware checkpoint compression#

Link negotiates both ordinary block compression (Features bit 128) and Frame schema grouping (bit 256, requiring 128). It obtains the fixed Frame schema and canonical section offset from its checkpoint codec. Both endpoints validate the same plan fingerprint. Grouped candidates are selected only when smaller; ordinary compression and original offers remain available. Receiver reconstruction ends with the same raw archive SHA-256, canonical envelope and typed checkpoint checks. Archive identity, retention and coordinator authority decisions remain unchanged.

The transfer contract describes layout lifetimes, bounded scratch and statistics. Low-level sender_publish can use a caller-owned codec for grouping; Link manages this automatically. The earlier experimental early-send schedules are not installed: gameplay and recovery retain their normal service order and the coordinator still enforces the configured rollback limit.

Checkpoint delivery channel#

Features bit 512 advertises support for checkpoint messages on the existing reliable channel. Link uses it when available; absent capability retains the unreliable path. The receiver mirrors reliable delivery after validating traffic, and cannot be downgraded by delayed datagrams in the same scope. Capabilities are immutable for a connection and reset on reconnect. Raw/compressed/schema-grouped archives all retain the same descriptors and validation.

For RTC this separates checkpoints from the unreliable snapshot credit window. It does not add credits, widen staging queues, change the shared byte budget, or prioritize checkpoints ahead of gameplay. Reliable chunk retries belong to the transport; the archive sender does not duplicate them. Reliable congestion can still delay gameplay on that channel, so callers must inspect actual backup age and failure state. A fresh replica is never an unconditional guarantee.
